title: Informal Conjecture (Introduction) — analogue of Kneser's theorem
statement_text: Maybe something like the following is true (the authors' original 'wild conjecture' that the upper bound $\phi(x,y)\le \frac{\lceil kx\rceil+\lceil ky\rceil-1}{k}$, valid for every integer $k\ge 1$, is always attained turns out to be false, 'but perhaps not ridiculously false'): for all $x, y \in (0, 1]$, there is an integer $k > 0$ with $\phi(x, y) = \frac{\lceil kx \rceil + \lceil ky \rceil - 1}{k}$.
context_text: A tripartition of a graph $G$ is a partition $(A,B,C)$ of $V(G)$ into three nonempty stable sets. For $x,y\in(0,1]$, $G$ is $(x,y)$-constrained via $(A,B,C)$ if every vertex of $A$ has at least $x|B|$ neighbours in $B$, every vertex of $B$ has at least $y|C|$ neighbours in $C$, and there are no edges between $A$ and $C$. For a vertex $v$, $N^2_A(v)$ is the set of vertices of $A$ at distance exactly two from $v$. $\phi(x,y)$ is the maximum $z$ such that every $(x,y)$-constrained graph (via some $(A,B,C)$) has a vertex $v\in C$ with $|N^2_A(v)|\ge z|A|$ (the maximum exists). Trivially $\phi(x,y)\ge\max(x,y)$, and a circulant construction on three sets of size $k$ gives $\phi(x,y)\le\frac{\lceil kx\rceil+\lceil ky\rceil-1}{k}$ for every integer $k\ge1$. The authors were motivated by extending Kneser's theorem from additive group theory to a general graph-theoretic setting; the conjecture that this upper bound is always tight is false, but they suggest that something like it may still be true, leaving the correct characterisation of $\phi(x,y)$ open.
notes: The 'wild conjecture' itself is explicitly stated to be false; only the informal residual belief 'maybe something like it is true' survives as an open direction. PDF source — math notation garbled in extraction (e.g. the formula for 1.3 reads as '⌈kx⌉ + 1 ⌉ − ky⌈ k' in the raw text).

title: Open Question — symmetry of $\psi$ (biconstrained case)
statement_text: Does $\psi(x, y) = \psi(y, x)$ hold for all $x, y \in (0, 1]$?
context_text: A tripartition of a graph $G$ is a partition $(A,B,C)$ of $V(G)$ into three nonempty stable sets. For $x,y\in(0,1]$, $G$ is $(x,y)$-constrained via $(A,B,C)$ if every vertex of $A$ has at least $x|B|$ neighbours in $B$, every vertex of $B$ has at least $y|C|$ neighbours in $C$, and there are no edges between $A$ and $C$; it is $(x,y)$-biconstrained if moreover every vertex of $B$ has at least $x|A|$ neighbours in $A$ and every vertex of $C$ has at least $y|B|$ neighbours in $B$. For a vertex $v$, $N^2_A(v)$ is the set of vertices of $A$ at distance exactly two from $v$. $\phi(x,y)$ is the maximum $z$ such that every $(x,y)$-constrained graph has a vertex $v\in C$ with $|N^2_A(v)|\ge z|A|$, and $\psi(x,y)$ is the same maximum taken over $(x,y)$-biconstrained graphs (both maxima exist, and $\phi\le\psi$). The authors prove, via a linear-programming argument, that $\phi(x,y)=\phi(y,x)$ for all $x,y\in(0,1]$, and remark that they have been unable to establish the analogous symmetry for $\psi$, although they have no counterexample.
notes: Stated as a prose remark following Theorem 2.3: 'we have not been able to prove an analogue of 2.3 for the biconstrained case, or for the exact case, although we have no counterexample for either one.' No labelled theorem environment.

title: Open Question — symmetry of $\xi$ (exact case)
statement_text: Does $\xi(x, y) = \xi(y, x)$ hold for all $x, y \in (0, 1]$?
context_text: Alongside the biconstrained question, the authors note that the symmetry $\phi(x,y)=\phi(y,x)$ has not been proved for the exact function $\xi$ either. They have no counterexample, and remark that one might hope $\xi$ (the 'nicest' of the three functions) is better-behaved than $\phi$.
